core: Continent-continent collision building fold-and-thrust mountains (Himalayas as the classic example)
Ocean-continent convergence lifting continental margins and building volcanic arcs (Andes, Cascades) and island arcs
Fault-block mountains from extensional tectonics (Basin and Range)
Uplift versus erosion as competing processes shaping ranges
Isostasy and isostatic rebound explained simply
Crustal thickening as the reason high mountains exist
Timescales: mountain building is slow, operating over millions of years
supporting: Thrust faults as low-angle reverse faults in fold-thrust belts
Normal faults and horst-and-graben structure in extension
Subduction zones and trenches as convergent-margin features
Quantitative examples: Everest height, Tibetan Plateau elevation, Challenger Deep depth, Basin and Range relief and extension
outOfScope: Plate tectonics theory and plate-boundary classification (plate-tectonics and plate-boundaries topics)
Volcanic processes, eruption styles, and hazards (volcanoes topic)
Weathering, erosion, and deposition mechanics (surface-processes topic)
Rock classification and metamorphism detail (rocks topics)

claims.claim: Continent-continent collision builds the highest mountain ranges: continental crust is relatively light and resists subduction, so the crust buckles and is pushed upward and sideways.
The Himalayas formed where India collided with Asia about 50 million years ago, and most of the range's growth occurred during the past 10 million years.
The Himalayas reach about 8,850 m (about 29,000 ft) above sea level and the Tibetan Plateau averages about 4,600 m in elevation; both figures are from USGS (peaks 'as high as 8,854 m').

In ocean-continent convergence the oceanic plate subducts beneath the continent, a deep trench forms, and the continental margin is uplifted; the Andes (Nazca Plate under South America) are the classic example, with volcanic arcs such as the Cascades on the overriding plate.
Oceanic-oceanic convergence builds curved chains of island arcs (e.g., Mariana and Aleutian Islands) as erupted material accumulates until submarine volcanoes rise above sea level.

Thrust faults, a special type of reverse fault with a low-angle fault plane, are common in fold-thrust belts created by continent-continent collision and can displace thick sheets of rock tens of kilometers.

Fault-block mountains form where the crust is stretched: normal faults raise some blocks and drop others. The Basin and Range province's crust has been extended up to 100% of its original width, with local relief up to about 10,000 ft (about 3,000 m).

Isostasy: the crust floats on the denser mantle (crust about 2.6 g/cm3, mantle about 3.4 g/cm3); adding mass through mountain building pushes the crust deeper, and removing mass through erosion lets it rebound over tens of millions of years.

Uplift and erosion compete: rising ranges are immediately attacked by weathering and erosion, and sediment washes into the adjacent valleys; summit height records what remains after erosion, not total uplift.
Mountain building is slow: plate motions of a few centimeters per year (e.g., about 2.5 cm/yr at the Mid-Atlantic Ridge) produce large changes only over millions of years.
Challenger Deep, at nearly 11,000 m below sea level, is deeper than Mount Everest is high (about 8,850 m).

conflictingEvidence.issue: Everest's height figure: USGS This Dynamic Earth states peaks 'as high as 8,854 m', while the 2020 Nepal-China joint survey announced 8,848.86 m.
positions: USGS source figure of 8,854 m (used in this lesson, phrased as 'about 8,850 m (about 29,000 ft)').
2020 official survey value of 8,848.86 m (not verifiable in the Tier A/B sources read for this lesson).
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson uses the USGS figure phrased as 'about 8,850 m (about 29,000 ft)', which is consistent with the cited source and arithmetically checked (8,854 m equals about 29,049 ft). The 2020 value was not asserted because no Tier A/B source read for this topic supplied it.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Steady versus uneven growth of the Himalayas.
positions: Growth spread evenly across the 50-million-year collision.
USGS states most growth occurred during the past 10 million years.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson describes orogeny as slow and uneven, citing the USGS statement that most Himalaya growth occurred in the past 10 million years.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft's boilerplate framing ('Mountain Building is a label on a toolbox drawer', 'a foundational concept students use to organize information') has no evidence basis and was discarded.
The draft's generic worked example ('a student reads a short scenario and identifies details that matter') was replaced with a source-verified Himalaya example.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced all generic draft prose with source-verified content on orogeny, fault-block mountains, isostasy, and timescales.
Everest's height is stated from the USGS figure (about 8,850 m / about 29,000 ft) rather than any unsourced modern value.
Scope restricted: plate-boundary classification, volcanic processes, and erosion/weathering mechanics are referenced only and left to sibling topics (plate-boundaries, volcanoes, surface-processes).

Every quantitative figure (Everest 8,854 m; Tibetan Plateau 4,600 m; Challenger Deep ~11,000 m; Basin and Range 10,000 ft and up-to-100% extension; crust 2.6 vs mantle 3.4 g/cm3; 2.5 cm/yr equals 25 km per million years) was re-checked arithmetically.

sourceRecords.title: Understanding Plate Motions
sourceRecords.notes: Read live on 2026-08-21 (This Dynamic Earth). Supports convergent-boundary mountain building: Andes uplift from Nazca subduction, island arcs from oceanic-oceanic convergence, Himalayas from the India-Asia collision at 50 Ma with most growth in the past 10 Ma, peaks as high as 8,854 m, Tibetan Plateau average about 4,600 m, Challenger Deep nearly 11,000 m, and the 2.5 cm/yr Mid-Atlantic Ridge spreading rate (25 km per million years). Record id reused from the phase-3 source registry (identical URL).

sourceRecords.title: Geologic Provinces of the United States: Basin and Range Province
sourceRecords.notes: The live host (geomaps.wr.usgs.gov) now redirects to a generic USGS shell page, so an Internet Archive capture of the original page (2006 snapshot) was read. Supports crustal extension of up to 100% of original width, normal-fault uplift of ranges and down-drop of valleys, roughly north-south trending faults, local relief up to 10,000 ft, the province's extent from eastern California to central Utah and southern Idaho into Sonora, Mexico, and immediate erosion of rising ranges with sediment filling the valleys.

sourceRecords.title: 9.4 Isostasy - Physical Geology
sourceRecords.notes: The live site is Cloudflare-blocked, so an Internet Archive capture (2019 snapshot) was read. Supports isostasy as the crust floating on the denser mantle (crust about 2.6 g/cm3, mantle about 3.4 g/cm3), crust sinking deeper as mountain building adds mass, rebound over tens of millions of years as erosion removes mass, and the glacial loading example (Greenland ice over 2,500 m thick; rebound likely to take more than 10,000 years).

sourceRecords.title: 10.4 Plates, Plate Motions, and Plate-Boundary Processes - Physical Geology (2nd edition)
sourceRecords.notes: The live site is Cloudflare-blocked, so an Internet Archive capture (2020 snapshot) was read. Supports the Andes and Cascade Range as subduction-built ranges, continent-continent collision with continental crust too light to subduct, the Himalaya from the India-Eurasia collision shortly after 50 Ma, the Alps-Zagros belt from the Africa-Eurasia collision, and the Rocky Mountains (B.C. and Alberta) as a continent-continent collision product.

sourceRecords.title: 12.3 Fracturing and Faulting - Physical Geology
sourceRecords.notes: The live site is Cloudflare-blocked, so an Internet Archive capture (2019 snapshot) was read. Supports normal faults as the product of extension, reverse faults as the product of compression, thrust faults (low-angle reverse faults) as common in fold-thrust belts created by continent-continent collision with tens of kilometers of displacement, and graben-and-horst structures in extensional settings.
